title: Microsoft AI Diagnoses 83% of Complex Cases, Beating Generalist Doctors in Study
excerpt: MAI-DxO, a panel of AI agents that questions patients and orders tests step by step, more than doubled generalist accuracy in a Science study — with specialists excluded and real-world trials still ahead.
body:
• Microsoft's MAI-DxO system correctly diagnosed 83% of complex New England Journal of Medicine cases in a peer-reviewed Science study, against 36% for generalist doctors working alone with reference materials.
  • The system works as a panel of AI agents that question a patient, order tests and debate a diagnosis step by step, rather than answering a single exam-style question.
  • The comparison excluded specialists and physician teams, who would normally handle cases this complex, and the cases were simulations, not live patients.
  • Microsoft is now moving to real-world evaluation with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and a healthcare foundation model with Mayo Clinic planned for next year.

Microsoft's AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases more than twice as often as generalist physicians in a simulation, according to a peer-reviewed study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, called the result a step toward "medical superintelligence," a term Microsoft defines as the capacity to surpass the strongest human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.

The system, called MAI-DxO, coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests and revise a working diagnosis as results come in. That step-by-step method is the point of the research: most medical AI has been graded on licensing-exam questions where every fact is handed over at once, a format no real patient presents in.

How the benchmark worked

To test the approach, Microsoft's team turned 304 complex cases published in the New England Journal of Medicine into sequential challenges in a benchmark called SDBench. Findings were revealed only when the AI or the doctor asked for them, and the estimated cost of every test counted against the final score. MAI-DxO reached the correct diagnosis in 83% of those cases. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with textbooks and reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. On emergency-department cases, the system scored about 80%, against about 47% for physicians.

Microsoft tested the orchestrator with models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and DeepSeek. Its best results came with OpenAI's GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. The study's own data shows much of the gain came from the underlying models, with the orchestration layer adding gains on top. GPT-5 alone, with a basic prompt, scored 78.9% on the complex cases at an estimated cost of about $8,400 a case; adding MAI-DxO cut roughly $3,000 from that bill and lifted accuracy by about four points. With GPT-5.5, the orchestrator raised accuracy on complex cases from 72% to nearly 87%, though it made little difference on emergency cases, where both approaches scored about 85%. Weaker models gained the most: Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash rose from 46.4% to nearly 69% with the orchestrator.

"The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise."

— Dominic King, Vice President of Health, Microsoft AI

The caveats in the result

The headline gap needs its context. Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or by teams of physicians, and neither was part of the comparison. The doctors tested were generalists working alone. The cases were also simulations built from published case records, not live patients in a clinic. In Microsoft's earlier preprint in June 2025, physicians who were barred from search engines and AI tools averaged about 20%, which shows how much the comparison conditions move the human score.

That does not make the result trivial. Diagnosis is where expertise is scarcest and errors are costly. But it is a benchmark result, not evidence the system is ready to diagnose patients unsupervised.

What Microsoft does next

Microsoft is moving the system toward real-world evaluation. Through a partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, patients will receive standard care while those who consent also engage with MAI-DxO in parallel, so researchers can compare its recommendations with those of treating doctors across emergency and urgent-care settings. King said Microsoft expects it to be the biggest study of its kind.

Suleyman told TechCrunch the company is also working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees diagnostic decision support as the expansion. A fuller account of the study and its limits is also covered by Human Resources Director, which examines what the result means for clinical training and accountability.

For health systems, the immediate question is not replacement but supervision: who signs off on an AI-assisted diagnosis, and what evidence regulators will require before a tool like this touches live care. The Boston evaluation is designed to start answering that.
